title: N-S-A
hookLine: nasa: to lift, to carry, as in Naso

lines: EACH FACE, ONE AT A TIME.
cards: When the Torah counts people, it doesn't always use a word for counting. In the portion called Naso, God tells Moses: "Take also the sum of the sons of Gershon." The Hebrew is naso et rosh: lift up the head.
To count someone, in that phrasing, is to raise their head, to see each face, one at a time.
Later in the same portion comes a blessing that lifts something else: "The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Today's root does the lifting in both.

teach.h: I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.
teach.b: N-S-A. Nun, sin, alef. Nasa: to lift, to carry, to bear.
First, the eyes. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." I will lift is essa, from this root.
Lifting begins with where you look. Second, the shoulders.
In the same portion, Naso, the Levites of Kohath carry the holy things of the sanctuary, and the text says they bore them upon their shoulders: the same verb.

The leaders of the tribes in that portion are called nesi'im, from these letters too. Third, forgiveness. When God's attributes are proclaimed to Moses, one of them is "forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin."

The Hebrew for forgiving there is nosei: carrying. To forgive, in this root, is to lift a wrong off someone and bear it. Cain uses the same verb from the other side, in despair: "My punishment is greater than I can bear."
Too heavy to lift. Fourth, the hands.
When the priests bless the people with the words from Naso, the practice is called nesiat kapayim, the lifting of the hands.
So one root raises heads to be counted, eyes to the hills, holy things onto shoulders, wrongs off backs, and hands in blessing.
In this root, lifting and carrying and forgiving are one motion.

how: The Torah portion Naso (Numbers 4:21–7:89) takes its name from 'naso et rosh', lift up the head; it includes the priestly blessing, which the priests give with raised hands, nesiat kapayim. Exodus 34:7 uses the same verb for forgiving.

o: the Hebrew root of lifting, carrying, forgiving
the Hebrew root of counting and numbers
the Hebrew root of a journey, setting out

p: lift up the head: take the sum
I will lift up mine eyes
the lifting of the priests' hands

s: in Naso, counting is phrased as lifting the head
naso et rosh: take the sum, lift up the head.
the Hebrew for forgiving in Exodus 34:7 has nothing to do with carrying
nosei: forgiving iniquity is carrying it.
the priestly blessing asks God to lift up his countenance
"The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."

games.q: you're Cain, sentenced to wander the earth. what do you say to God?
o: my punishment is greater than I can bear.
games.why: "My punishment is greater than I can bear": too heavy to lift, with today's verb. and God sets a mark on him, so that no one would kill him.

practice: Let your shoulders rise on an in-breath and drop on the out-breath, a few times, slowly.
Then ask what someone near you is carrying that you could lift a little, a chore, a worry, a grudge you could set down, or choose a weight of your own to put down for now.

If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills. And if something ever feels too heavy to bear alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: N-S-A. Nun, sin, alef: nasa, to lift, to carry, to forgive. And this week's lines, in order: the world hides, exile reveals, sit and learn, friendship joins, dawn, we stand surety, lift. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: to lift, carry, bear, from nun, sin, alef; Naso, 'lift up', names a Torah portion.

carryVoice: Your line: lift. Eyes first, then shoulders, then hands. Same time tomorrow.
